subject: Scaling playbook — perf/SLO recap & next steps

Subject: Scaling playbook — perf/SLO recap & next steps

Hi Eric — thanks again for the call today. Quick written recap so we have a single source of truth and clear next steps. Short version first, details below.

High-level SLOs you described
- 95p latency target: < 300ms for short-chat flows (<= 256 tokens)
- Sustained throughput target: ~200 requests/sec for typical daytime load
- Concurrency target: tolerate 600 concurrent connections across regions (spiky fan-out)
- Streaming: client-level streaming required for low-latency token delivery; connection reuse/session affinity preferred

Autoscaling & burst expectations we discussed
- Warm pool idea: keep a small pre-warmed set of workers to serve sudden bursts with minimal cold-starts
- Burst capacity: want ability to handle 3x baseline short spikes (i.e., ~600 rps) for up to ~2 minutes
- Scale-up time target: ideally under 90s for GPU-backed workers; prefer 30–60s for common code paths
- Queueing/backpressure: prefer limited in-service queuing (short queuing window + client retry guidance) vs long external queues

Immediate next steps (proposed)
1) We'll share a scaling playbook + load-test plan (attached) for you to review.
2) Connor/Markus to propose warm-pool sizing and an initial autoscale policy based on your traffic shape.
3) Run a short perf probe (script attached) against a dev/preview model to validate latency percentiles and scale-up behavior.
4) Workshop on Thu Apr 9, 11:00 AM PT to walk results and finalize canary plan.

Questions I still have (for your team)
- Any hard SLA/billing constraints for burst minutes (e.g., internal budget cap)?
- Do you need guaranteed concurrency isolation per-customer/tenant?

Attachments: scaling_playbook_v1.pdf, load_test_plan.xlsx, perf_probe_script.sh

Thanks — Neha

Thanks Neha — very helpful summary. A couple quick clarifications from our side: 

1) Budget constraints: we can accept burst minutes but would like visibility into cost delta; is there a way to estimate incremental cost for 3x bursts for 2 minutes?
2) Cold starts: when you say 30–60s, is that the time to get a GPU worker fully ready (model loaded + KV cache warmed)? We need to understand worst-case cold-starts for planning fallback UX.
3) Concurrency isolation: yes, we'd prefer soft isolation (fair queueing per-tenant) rather than hard allocation unless cost justifies it.

Also confirm that your perf probe won't hit our prod traffic — we'll provide a preview cluster and a pair of test keys.

Hi Eric — Markus from the infra team here, adding some technical detail so our workshop can be focused. Long-ish but wanted to be explicit about tradeoffs.

Cold-start vs warm-pool
- Cold-start baseline: provisioning a new GPU instance and loading a 13B-ish model (quantized) typically completes in ~60–120s depending on image pull/cache hit and host instability. Model load itself is 20–45s on our optimized path.
- Warm-pool strategy: keep a small number of pre-warmed worker processes with the model loaded but without hot KV caches; warm-pool entry allows serving in ~5–15s for non-KV-heavy flows.
- KV cache priming: for chat flows with long prefixes the KV cache matters; we can prime caches proactively for common session prefixes during a burst window to reduce initial 95p latency. Priming cost is modest (network + token generation) but must be part of the load test.

Autoscale policy suggestion (initial)
- Baseline pool: sized to handle average steady-state 200 rps with 20% headroom
- Warm pool: 5–10% of baseline workers (auto-adjust by traffic percentile) to give sub-15s response for most bursts
- Reactive scale-up: add GPU-backed workers in small batches (10–20% of baseline) with a scale-up cooldown of 30–45s between steps to avoid flapping
- Burst cap: allow temporary over-provisioning to 3x baseline for up to 120s before triggering longer-term scale decisions

Queueing & backpressure
- We recommend short in-service buffers (per-worker request queues capped to N requests) with immediate 429/503 guidance to clients beyond that window. This keeps tail latency bounded and pushes retry behavior to the client side.
- For streaming flows we preserve a persistent connection and provide per-stream backpressure signals; our runtime supports incremental token flush to reduce perceived latency.

Observability and cost estimation
- We'll provide per-minute cost estimates for warm-pool vs reactive scaling using your expected traffic curve — this will be part of the load-test deliverable.

I'll attach a quick profiling log from a 13B load test we ran (summary below) and will prepare an initial HPA-style policy you can review before the workshop.

Profiling summary (example)
- Cold model load: 78s (image pull 20s, model load 38s, init kernels 20s)
- Warm-pool serve time: median 22ms, 95p 180ms for 64-token short-completions (with streaming enabled)
- Peak memory usage: 34GB per worker (quantized)

Happy to dig into any of the above on Thu.

—Markus
